note: Supplementary measurements beyond the head-to-head suite. Each entry names the script that reproduces it. The trait-count sweep was re-measured for every library on 2026-09-06, after distinct generated sources landed in apecs; the competitors moved only within run-to-run noise, their versions having not changed. Sorted-query figures were re-measured after orderBy landed.

traitCountSweep.script: node cliff-cross.mjs <library> <k>   (one k per process, deliberately)
traitCountSweep.what: ns per entity-visit, ergonomic tier: N=1000 entities carrying k distinct traits, one pass per trait.

apecsBeforeDistinctSources.what: The same measurement before src/core/codegen.ts distinct() landed (2026-09-06). Identical generated source made V8 hand every driver and cursor the same SharedFunctionInfo, so the per-query codegen shared one feedback vector and the sites inside it went megamorphic.

apecsCallCost.what: Fixed cost per call plus marginal cost per entity, single-trait query. Re-measured 2026-09-06: unchanged by the accessor work and by the distinct-source fix — a one-trait query has no shape collision to lose.

sortedQueries.what: 100 000 entities iterated in sorted order every frame, microseconds. Every apecs frame includes the world.step() a real frame pays: the dirty check is tick-based (SPEC 8.3), so a view only settles once the tick has moved past the writes that built it.
sortedQueries.note: orderBy (SPEC 6.8) permutes the archetype rows themselves, so a clean frame is the plain chunk walk and nothing else: 0.89 ns/entity against the 26.3 ns/entity the materialised sortBy walk costs. The previous figures in this file were measured without world.step(), which left the sortBy view resorting every frame in the static regime.

sortedIsolation.what: Same query, same data: linear vs sorted iteration, ns per entity. Still open.

sortedStaticIsLinear.what: sorted.entities() on a view whose keys were never touched. SPEC 12.1 budgets zero work; cost is flat per entity at every size, i.e. O(n).

coalescing.what: becsy defers structural changes to the frame boundary, so in-frame add+remove could have been collapsed to nothing. It is not.

silentTruncation.what: becsy's perf build has assertions compiled out. On default maxShapeChangesPerFrame it silently creates only some of the entities requested and every query built on them comes back short, with no error. Caught by census.mjs; fixed by sizing the limits explicitly in the adapter.

randomAccessBreakdown.what: apecs random_access split apart, ns per entity, after the Tier 1 cleanup AND the removal of sparse storage. Was 51.9 before either; 30.8 after Tier 1 alone.

accessor.what: world.accessor() against the prototypes that motivated it. The earlier '8.8 ns ceiling' compared a FUSED read-modify-write against a two-call get+set, and used a one-entry cache that collapses under fragmentation -- it was not a like-for-like target. Against a like-for-like dense-table prototype the shipped accessor is within 2 ns.

layoutQuestion.question: Would giving the accessor bitECS's structure (a flat array indexed by entity id) reach bitECS's 1.3x?
layoutQuestion.answer: No -- and the premise is wrong. At the pure-memory level the archetype indirection is not slower than a flat id-indexed array (1.43 vs 1.79 ns), so the layout is not what costs apecs. The 14.8 ns is software above the access path.
layoutQuestion.note: The sparse-storage middle ground referenced here has since been removed from apecs, so table storage is the only layout.

sparseRemoval.what: storage: 'sparse' was removed. Effect on the head-to-head, comparing merged 3-run figures before and after: neutral to slightly positive, with the structural benchmarks gaining most as branches left the add/remove path. Nothing regressed.
sparseRemoval.getSetPath: 30.8 -> 26.5 ns/entity, the sparse branch leaving World#get / #set
sparseRemoval.testsAfter: 1353 passed, 76 skipped; bundle 125 398 B raw / 34 568 B gzip
